newsitem.title: FRANCE: Next EU parliament president already known.
newsitem.headline: Next EU parliament president already known.

text.p: Jose Maria Gil-Robles of Spain will become the next President of the European Parliament in January, under a deal carved out on Wednesday by the right of centre European People's Party (EPP).
The party chose Gil-Robles as its candidate which means the assembly will be faced with an effective "fait accompli" when the vote is held in January.

Under the parliament's system of wheeling and dealing its two main parties -- the Socialists and EPP -- divide up the increasingly high-profile presidency between them, to the frustration of smaller groups like the Liberals and Greens.

Gil-Robles, a member of the Spanish Partido Popular, will succeed Klaus Haensch, a German Social Democrat, under a pact giving the 215-strong Socialist Group the first half of the five year term and the 182-strong EPP the second.
But the horse-trading did not stop there. To the wrath of smaller countries the choice of Gil-Robles was settled in a secret agreement between the two big countries in the group -- Spain and Germany.

The bigger countries have more members in the assembly and parliamentary sources said Spanish deputies only backed the election of German EPP member Egon Klepsch, the last EPP president, in 1992 on condition it was their turn next.

France's Nicole Fontaine, a rival candidate backed by French President Jacques Chirac who dropped out of the race in frustration on Wednesday, did not hide her disdain for the deal between Germany and Spain.
"I do not want to be the alibi for this parody of democracy," she told reporters.
The only other contender was Greece's Georgios Anastassopoulos.
Gil-Robles, a lawyer who was a legal official for the Spanish government under late dictator Francisco Franco, will lead the 626-member parliament up to the next elections in June 1999.

The Dutch leader of the parliament's Liberal Group, Gijs de Vries, said he might put up a candidate to challenge Gil-Robles, but admitted to reporters that the smaller groups were powerless to stop the two major groups.
